open_obligations: Check which design difference (hidden passage, interaction, baseline) explains the different conclusions.
Note that Michael et al. have no no-argument baseline, so the two results answer different comparisons.
Check that both use QuALITY questions of comparable difficulty (hard subsets).
in.other_title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert judges: 84% vs 74% on hard reading comprehension questions
in.rationale: Parrish et al. conclude that, for reading comprehension, debate is not a helpful format, since judges perform similarly with or without two-turn arguments. Michael et al. report 84% judge accuracy for interactive human debate versus 74% for consultancy on QuALITY-hard; settings differ sharply: Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage, debates are interactive and unbounded, and the baseline is consultancy rather than no arguments.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate is a helpful format for human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension

open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51 to check whether the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Check that Parrish et al.'s two-turn judges had time-limited passage access, unlike Michael et al.'s judges
Compare the baselines: Parrish et al. compare with a no-argument condition; check whether Michael et al. compare with consultancy
in.other_title: Unbounded-length debates differ from Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn QuALITY setting
in.rationale: Parrish et al.'s two-turn study (one argument plus one counter-argument) reports that humans perform similarly with or without arguments. Michael et al. note that in Parrish et al.'s experiments debate does not significantly improve judge accuracy and point to differences between the settings, first that their own debates are unbounded in length, which they suggest may have produced more useful and informative arguments, so the challenge is scoped to protocol.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether multi-turn debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the contrast depends on protocol differences, first debate length (unbounded in Michael et al., bounded at a single refutation in Parrish et al.)

open_obligations: Note that two turns is still far from unbounded interactive debate.
Check that the follow-up's judges and time limits are comparable to those of the original study.
Check whether judges could read enough of the passage to bypass the arguments.
Check that the follow-up uses 2-option QuALITY questions with human-written arguments, since the cited passages do not say so.
out.other_title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
out.rationale: Parrish et al. (single-turn) ask whether a multi-turn setting with counterarguments is needed. The two-turn follow-up adds a second round of counter-arguments and reports that humans perform similarly regardless of whether they have access to arguments.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether adding explicit counter-arguments makes debate helpful to human judges, on the two-turn follow-up's reading comprehension task

text: The authors test whether adding a second round of counter-arguments to single-turn debate arguments helps human judges answer reading comprehension questions, and report that humans perform similarly on their task regardless of whether they have access to arguments. They say these findings suggest that, in the case of answering reading comprehension questions, debate is not a helpful format.
title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments did not help humans on the authors' reading comprehension task
